title: Readiness probes fail during a normal traffic spike
description: Diagnose how a readiness probe that depends on a shared resource can cause cascading pod removals during a traffic spike, turning a load increase into a service outage.

data.text: A readiness probe is supposed to protect users from being routed to a pod that cannot handle requests. But when the probe itself depends on a shared resource—a database connection pool, a thread pool, or a downstream API—it can become the trigger for cascading failure. Under load, the probe times out, Kubernetes removes the pod from the service endpoints, and the remaining pods absorb more traffic, causing their probes to fail, and so on. The system enters a death spiral where healthy pods are removed faster than they can recover.

data.title: Core concepts
items: Readiness probe: determines if a pod should receive traffic, not whether it is alive
Endpoint Slice: Kubernetes resource tracking ready pod IPs for a service
Load shedding: an application pattern that rejects requests when resources are constrained
PodDisruptionBudget: limits how many pods can be unavailable simultaneously
Cascading removal: when failing probes remove pods from service, concentrating traffic on fewer pods

terms.definition: A Kubernetes probe that determines whether a container is ready to accept traffic. Failed probes remove the pod from service endpoints.
A Kubernetes resource that tracks the set of ready pod IPs for a service, updated based on readiness probe results.
An application pattern that rejects requests when resources are constrained, protecting the process from overload.
A Kubernetes resource that limits the number of pods that can be voluntarily or involuntarily disrupted at the same time.

items: Health check endpoint opens a database connection pool under load and times out
Readiness probe uses a tight timeout that is exceeded during CPU contention
Shared connection pool or thread pool is exhausted by the traffic spike
Probe hits a cold cache or unindexed query that degrades under concurrent load
HPA scales pods, but new pods fail readiness checks while warming up caches
Load balancer health check interval is shorter than the application warm-up time

cards.title: Increase Timeout and Delay
cards.description: Raise the readiness probe timeoutSeconds and initialDelaySeconds to tolerate slower responses.
cons: Slower detection of genuinely unhealthy pods
May keep unhealthy pods in rotation longer

cards.title: Decouple Health from Dependencies
cards.description: Make the readiness endpoint check only application-local state, not downstream databases.
cons: Requires a secondary liveness or synthetic monitor

cards.title: Application-Level Load Shedding
cards.description: Return 503 from the readiness endpoint when internal resource utilization exceeds a threshold.
pros: Signals the orchestrator to remove the pod

data.caption: Readiness probe behavior during a traffic spike
data.definition:
graph TD
    A[Traffic Spike] --> B[App Resource Pressure]
    B --> C{Readiness Probe}
    C -->|Pass| D[Pod Receives Traffic]
    C -->|Fail| E[Pod Removed from Endpoints]
    E --> F[Other Pods Overloaded]
    F --> G[More Probes Fail]
    G --> H[Cascading Removals]
    H --> I[Service Unavailable]

items: Check endpoint slice changes with kubectl get endpointslices to see pods being removed.
Review readiness probe configuration: timeout, period, successThreshold, and failureThreshold.
Inspect application metrics during the spike: CPU, memory, thread pool, and connection pool usage.
Run the health endpoint locally under load to reproduce the slow response.
Check if the health endpoint opens a new database connection on every request.

data.title: Do not put database checks in readiness
data.text: A readiness probe that verifies database connectivity can cause cascading failures. If the database is under load, every probe adds more load, and failing probes remove pods from service, concentrating traffic on fewer pods.

items: Keep readiness checks local: memory, thread state, and cache warmness
Use separate synthetic monitors for end-to-end dependency health
Set failureThreshold to 2 or 3 to tolerate transient slowness
Implement graceful degradation: serve cached data when the database is slow
Use PodDisruptionBudget to prevent too many pods from being removed simultaneously
Test probe behavior under load with a chaos engineering tool before production traffic

items.question: What is the difference between readiness and liveness probes?
items.answer: A liveness probe restarts the container when it fails. A readiness probe removes the pod from traffic without restarting it. Use readiness for temporary overload and liveness for permanent failure.

items.question: Can readiness probes cause downtime?
items.answer: If too many pods fail readiness simultaneously, yes. Use PodDisruptionBudget and conservative failure thresholds to prevent cascading removal.

data.title: Fix a readiness probe that causes cascading failures
data.description: An API gateway fails readiness probes during a marketing campaign traffic spike, causing 503 errors for all users. Diagnose and fix the probe configuration.
steps: Examine endpoint slice changes and pod removal timestamps
Review the readiness probe configuration and the health endpoint code
Identify whether the probe depends on a shared resource that degrades under load
Refactor the health endpoint to check only local state
Configure PodDisruptionBudget to limit concurrent pod removals
Deploy and verify the fix under simulated load
data.expectedOutcome: A readiness probe that reflects true application readiness without causing cascading failures during traffic spikes.

data.title: Summary
points: Readiness probes should be local and lightweight
Do not validate downstream dependencies in readiness checks
Use conservative failure thresholds to avoid transient failures
Protect against cascading removal with PodDisruptionBudget
Test probe behavior under realistic load before relying on it in production
data.takeaway: A readiness probe is a signal to the load balancer, not a comprehensive health check. Design it to be fast, local, and tolerant of transient conditions.
